Foundational models have demonstrated impressive general-purpose performance DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025) ; Grattafiori et al. (2024) . These models usually consist of billions of parameters, are trained on massive datasets, and have become the standard in modern deep learning. Empirical studies such as scaling laws have demonstrated that increasing model size generally leads to lower training loss Kaplan et al. (2020) ; Hoffmann et al. (2022) . However, training larger models requires significantly more compute, highlighting the need for more compute-efficient pre-training methods. Figure 1: Evaluation log-perplexity vs. log trainable parameters (non-embedding) across model sizes. BPT approaches the fully-parameterized baseline while using far fewer trainable parameters; on the 1.5B model it achieves comparable eval loss with 66% fewer trainable parameters

During training, a given trainable parameter incurs a fixed memory overhead: the parameter itself ( n n ), its gradient ( n n ), and two optimizer states ( 2 ​ n 2n ) when using Adam family of optimizers Kingma and Ba (2017) ; Loshchilov and Hutter (2019) . While total training memory depends on several factors such as batch size and activation footprint Chen et al. (2016) , this 4 ​ n 4n overhead remains fixed per trainable parameter. Distinguishing between non-trainable and trainable parameters for pre-training is important, and the total number of parameters can be interpreted as the model’s representational capacity. Our central claim is that effective pre-training does not require optimizing every parameter. Instead, models can retain much of the learning behavior of full training while updating only a small subset of parameters, provided that the resulting updates preserve the essential training dynamics. We first analyze the general learning dynamics of full-parameter training in terms of the rank of the update for SGD and Adam optimizers, showing that in full-parameter training, updates are high-rank, and verify this behavior on a simple model. Then, to preserve the learning dynamics of high-rank while being parameter-efficient, we introduce Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a novel parameter-efficient method for pre-training foundation models that updates a weight matrix W \mathrm{W} by simultaneously applying constrained high-rank and low-rank updates. This work directly builds on prior works such as LoRA Hu et al. (2021) , ReLoRA Lialin et al. (2023) , and HyperAdapt Gurung and Campbell (2025) and combines them in pre-training setting to achieve high-rank updates at every optimization step.

The claim that a high-rank update is necessary is consistent with prior evidence. ReLoRA Lialin et al. (2023) shows that allowing a brief period of full-parameter training before switching to low-rank adaptation improves optimization, suggesting early learning benefits from richer (higher-rank) update directions Lialin et al. (2023) . Complementarily, systematic ablations that increase LoRA rank r r toward full-rank updates report that doing this matches full training performance when the model is trained from scratch, reinforcing the link between update rank and training performance Huh et al. (2024) . Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by pre-training three language models of varying sizes, showing consistent performance across scales. We also perform a comprehensive downstream evaluation of the trained models to show that there is minimal performance loss when using fewer trainable parameters than when using all trainable parameters. Our main contributions are as follows: • We introduce Bi-Phase Training (BPT) to significantly reduce the number of trainable parameters required during pre-training. • We provide a theoretical upper-bound to the rank of the update induced by BPT. • We comprehensively test the method on downstream evaluation tasks and show that there is minimal performance difference between the fully parameterized training and BPT.

Our pre-training experiments at 10 billion tokens demonstrate BPT achieves validation perplexity close to full-parameter training across different model scales while achieving substantial reductions in trainable parameters. Figure 1 summarizes our experimental results across different model sizes. The x-axis represents the trainable parameters, not including embedding parameters. We show that, for a given model size, BPT achieves log-perplexity performance on a validation set similar to that of the full parameterized model, with significantly fewer trainable parameters. Figure 4 compares the evaluation log perplexity on the validation set for the Qwen-2.5-1.5B and OLMo-2 between the Full, ReLoRA, and BPT. We show that even with 66% less trainable parameters , BPT achieves validation loss close to full-parameter training. The log-perplexity of validation data shows that the model does not simply overfit the training data and has a similar evaluation loss profile as the baseline. Both BPT and ReLoRA have almost an identical number of trainable parameters. ReLoRA’s eval loss slowly diverges from BPT’s, even though both methods use a similar high learning rate. Figure 6: BPT ablations and memory summary. Left/Middle: rank and merge-frequency ablations on the 100M model trained on 10B tokens. Higher rank for the low-rank matrices leads to lower validation loss. Less frequent merges also lead to lower validation loss. Right: Peak GPU memory for Qwen-2.5-1.5B. BPT saves 5.8 GB to train a 1.5B model.

In this paper, we introduced Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a parameter-efficient pre-training method that combines diagonal high-rank transformations with periodically merged low-rank adapters. Across language-model pre-training from 100M to 1.5B parameters, BPT approaches full-training validation loss and preserves much of its downstream performance, while optimizing substantially fewer trainable parameters. This suggests that BPT can be a practical route to more efficient foundation-model pre-training.

passages.text: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node’s memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb ( D istributed O ptimizer with B lock-diagonal Eigen b ases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.

Language-model scaling increases the memory requirements for parameters, gradients, and optimizer state ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . When these quantities exceed a single GPU’s capacity, training distributes them across devices through tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) . Under either layout, each device holds one part of every sharded weight matrix, and we call this part a shard; data-parallel replicas hold copies of the same shards. Cross-shard communication is communication among the devices that hold different shards of one matrix. These layouts make matrix-aware optimization a distributed problem: an update defined on a complete weight matrix may require information held by several devices. Muon orthogonalizes momentum ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , which introduces dense optimizer-specific communication in conventional sharded implementations ( Ahn et al., 2025 ; Khaled et al., 2026 ) . MuonBP reduces communication by performing local Newton–Schulz orthogonalization between periodic global steps, but those global steps still require full cross-shard communication ( Khaled et al., 2026 ) . The frequency of global orthogonalization controls the tradeoff between communication cost and optimization quality. Another approach, Dion, reduces the size of each exchange by approximating momentum with low-rank factors and retaining the residual through error feedback ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . Its optimizer step communicates these factors across shards, so communication scales with the update rank.

In this work, we introduce Dobb ( D istributed O ptimizer with B lock-diagonal Eigen b ases) to reduce optimizer communication. We approximate the activation second moment by a block-diagonal matrix and retain a complete eigenbasis within every block. This construction discards cross-block correlations without imposing a reduced-rank constraint on the update. When these blocks align with shard boundaries, the optimizer step requires no cross-shard communication beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. Dion derives its low-rank factors from momentum; we instead project momentum onto an input-side basis from an exponentially averaged activation second moment, normalize the coefficients, and reconstruct the update. Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node’s memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb ( D istributed O ptimizer with B lock-diagonal Eigen b ases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. matches.abstract_excerpt: Grokking is a delayed transition from memorization to generalization in deep neural networks (NNs). passages.text: A stronger dense encoder preserves the distinction between finding a paper in the collection and selecting it among namesakes. passages.section: 4.4 Retrieval fields and stronger ranking functions
passages.text: The comparison keeps query evidence and document fields explicit. All title-only rows expose the same candidate text. Full-index search considers every indexed title, while exact-name ranking receives the complete observed namesake group. These scopes serve distinct stages of scientific search. A full-index retrieval score captures candidate discovery and target ranking together; exact-name ranking measures selection within a known group. The query demonstration exposes both the name group and the source record selected by research context. Adding the source abstract improves identification while preserving a smaller shared-name gap. With the same E5 encoder and the same three-term queries, title-plus-abstract retrieval reaches 87.9% Top-1 for shared-name targets and 94.8% for matched unique-name targets. The paired residual difference is 6.9 points [4.8, 9.0], compared with 15.3 points [11.6, 18.9] for E5 over titles. Within exact-name candidates, the richer field reaches 93.6% [92.3, 94.8]. The index now contains the abstract from which the query terms were extracted. This controlled field comparison measures how providing that evidence changes identification. The two interventions address different parts of the search task. Candidate restriction specifies which label group the reader intends; richer document fields supply evidence for distinguishing its members. Keeping their outcomes separate exposes both contributions. In the title-plus-abstract condition, exact-name selection reaches 93.6% against 87.9% full-index accuracy on the identical shared-name targets. Under title-only evidence, listwise ranking reaches 89.2% with the complete candidate group. These configurations provide concrete retrieval and reranking targets under explicit information budgets.

Scientific names increasingly converge across research topics. The version-aware corpus records 4.33-fold growth in cross-topic collision against 1.12-fold growth within topics, with the pattern reproduced by a second sentence encoder. Fixed frequency bands locate most of the increase in intermediate-frequency names. Source-linked PRISM, TRACE, and SAGE cases connect this population pattern to distinct scientific objects, observed spellings, and documented method lineages. Specific research clues recover many intended papers while leaving a measurable residual identification gap. Shared-name targets remain 25.7 points behind matched unique-name targets under title-based BM25 and 6.9 points behind under title-plus-abstract E5. Within complete same-name candidate sets, contextual ranking reaches 70.6% with BM25, 89.2% with a language model, and 93.6% with E5 over titles and abstracts. Topic-specific errors and fixed-size comparisons identify same-topic competitors as the harder ambiguity. The shared corpus, frozen queries, complete candidate groups, and 60,200 recorded outcomes make these comparisons directly reusable. Together, the findings support scientific search interfaces that expose namesakes, use research context to rank them, and preserve a verifiable paper identifier in the final result.

passages.text: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language-model training can exhibit large loss spikes with Muon-family optimizers. We introduce EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates routed-expert updates according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of their finite-step Newton–Schulz directions. EnergyCal leaves the spectral transform unchanged and adds no persistent optimizer state. We evaluate it on a 4B-parameter MoE model. Against a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, EnergyCal–MuonH reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06%, with a modest throughput cost. With plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay, the reduction in mean spike burden averages 95.98% across the two tested exponents, accompanied by small endpoint improvements. These findings support stabilization both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated setting.

Figure 1: EnergyCal overview. (1) Sparse routing creates uneven expert traffic. (2) Each routed matrix’s post-NS energy determines q e q_{e} ; when q e > 0 q_{e}>0 , scaling preserves the individual NS direction, not necessarily the displacement after Hyperball projection or writeback. (3) Continuous calibration reduces observed thresholded loss-spike burden. Curves are schematic, not measurements; coefficients use direction energy, not token counts. Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route tokens unevenly across experts, creating time-varying optimization conditions [ 1 ] . This setting can be challenging for Muon-family optimizers, which use Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations to transform momentum-based updates. Muon has shown promise for language-model pretraining [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] , while Hyperball introduces explicit control over weight and update norms [ 5 ] . Its Muon variant, MuonH, normalizes update directions and projects weights onto a fixed-radius sphere. In our custom 4B-parameter DeepSeekMoE-style model, both Muon and MuonH exhibit intermittent loss spikes, although all full-schedule runs complete. We investigate whether these loss excursions can be mitigated through a simple modification of routed-expert updates.

An expert can retain nonzero momentum even when no tokens are assigned to it in the current step. This motivates examining expert-wise update magnitudes, particularly under MuonH’s fixed-norm normalization. We propose EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates each routed-expert update according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of its finite-step NS direction. Figure 1 illustrates the method. The coefficient is bounded between zero and one and is applied continuously during training. EnergyCal leaves the NS transform, momentum, and router objective unchanged, requires no token-utilization statistics, and adds no persistent optimizer state. Its energy statistic is not scale-invariant stable rank: low energy can reflect direction concentration, amplitude, or both. We evaluate EnergyCal in two separate full-schedule studies, each using three initialization seeds. First, a frozen EnergyCal–MuonH recipe reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06% relative to a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, with 1.62% lower mean throughput. Second, applying EnergyCal to plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay reduces mean spike burden by 95.98% on average across the two tested exponents, with small endpoint improvements. Together, these results show that stabilization is observed both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated MoE setting. However, plain Muon retains intermediate-quality and speed advantages in the first study, and different evaluation banks prevent a direct ranking of the calibrated optimizer families.

Our contribution is an empirical evaluation of one-sided, post-NS energy attenuation across MuonH and plain Muon. Unlike utilization- or alignment-guided expert scaling methods [ 6 , 7 ] , EnergyCal relies only on the energy of each logical matrix’s NS direction. The results do not establish general optimizer superiority or identify the cause of individual spikes: single-update interventions fail to rescue two examined events, and the plain-Muon study lacks a routed-only uniform-scaling control to separate energy-dependent attenuation from a simpler reduction in update magnitude. We therefore focus on the measured stability benefits and their practical trade-offs within the tested setting; Section 7 discusses these evidence boundaries.

Scope, measurement, and generalizability. Both cohorts use one custom 4B-parameter, 128-expert, top-2 MoE model and 1.31B training tokens per run, with three initialization seeds and a shared data order. The results therefore do not establish generalization across architectures, scales, data distributions, or training budgets. Cohort H selects baselines within bounded learning-rate grids whose best-tested values lie at the lower boundaries; Cohort M fixes the plain-Muon recipe rather than independently retuning every variant. Reported standard deviations describe run-to-run variation, not confidence intervals. The adaptive spike detector can miss persistent loss elevation, while periodic validation may miss transient quality changes. Selected spectral measurements are not an all-layer census, and the local probes omit the subsequent router-bias-controller update.

Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank–distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA) , an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.

Foundation models are increasingly adapted into specialized models for a wide range of downstream tasks. Updating every parameter of these models, however, is costly to train, store, and deploy, particularly when many task-specific variants share the same foundation model. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) addresses this cost by learning only a small set of task-specific parameters while leaving the pretrained model frozen. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ Hu et al., 2022 ] has emerged as an especially effective form of PEFT. Rather than modifying a weight matrix directly, LoRA learns an additive update represented as the product of two low-rank factors. This parameterization can retain the benefits of task-specific fine-tuning with far fewer trainable and stored parameters, making each specialization a compact adapter that can be shared, composed with a common base model, and loaded on demand. A collection of LoRA adapters served from a shared base model forms a LoRA fleet . Modern inference frameworks increasingly support serving such fleets, with individual adapters selected or loaded on a per-request basis. Systems such as vLLM [ Kwon et al., 2023 ] , S-LoRA [ Sheng et al., 2024 ] , Punica [ Chen et al., 2024 ] , and LoRAX [ Predibase, 2023 ] enable such multi-LoRA serving by batching, routing, and managing adapters around shared base weights. At this scale, adapters compete for finite GPU cache capacity, transfer bandwidth, and rank-dependent inference resources. Compress-then-Serve shows that compressing an adapter fleet can translate into substantial serving gains [ Brüel-Gabrielsson et al., 2025 ] .

There is substantial capacity to reclaim from trained LoRA adapters. To characterize rank redundancy in the wild, we analyze 96,370 96{,}370 matrices from 200 popular LoRA repositories on Hugging Face and find that spectral energy is strongly concentrated: at τ = .90 \tau=.90 , the median layer retains only 31.2 % 31.2\% of its nominal rank (Fig. 1 ). This widespread redundancy makes post-hoc compression an attractive way to reduce adapter memory, transfer volume, and rank-dependent serving overhead, allowing a fixed serving capacity to accommodate a larger adapter fleet [ Vasani et al., 2025 , Kumaravelu et al., 2026 , Brüel-Gabrielsson et al., 2025 , He et al., 2026 ] . The challenge, however, is no longer simply whether rank can be removed, but how a limited rank budget should be allocated. Within a single adapter, different layers need not tolerate the same degree of truncation. Accordingly, the available rank should be distributed to preserve the adapter’s behavior as well as possible. At fleet scale, the problem becomes coupled, as adapters share the same serving capacity yet may differ substantially in how much compression they can tolerate. Effective post-hoc compression must therefore decide both how rank is divided across layers and how the shared budget is divided across adapters.

We address this two-level allocation problem with Functional Rank Allocation (FRA) . For each adapter, the ideal objective is a functional rank–distortion frontier that captures the minimum behavioral change achievable at every retained-rank budget. Constructing this frontier exactly is combinatorial, so FRA uses end-to-end measurements of individual module truncations to form an additive search surrogate and solves the resulting rank-allocation problem exactly by dynamic programming. Each proposed allocation is then instantiated and remeasured end to end, so the surrogate is used only to generate candidates rather than to assign their final risk. Because the additive surrogate can be calibrated differently across allocation shapes, FRA also evaluates a complementary spectral candidate and retains the lower-risk allocation at each budget. The resulting measured frontiers are finally coupled through exact minimax allocation over these constructed frontiers under the shared rank budget. Reranking improves relevance but adds latency, so teams look for faster alternatives. System-1-style decision models make direct, structured predictions instead of generating long responses. We first screen 21 open-weight models on 11 benchmarks, then compare a promising decision model with a dedicated reranker on identical candidate lists. The default decision-model setup fails on many long candidate sets, so scoring only the requests it completes gives a misleading ranking. Limiting candidate text length largely restores reliability and makes some configurations competitive. A frozen evaluation on new retrieval data supports the reliability and ranking results, but confirms the latency requirement for only one of the two selected configurations. Across workloads, which model ranks better changes, and a tuned reranker remains faster and uses far less GPU memory. A decision model can perform competitive reranking, but replacing a reranker requires weighing quality, latency and memory together, and teams should tune the reranker they already run first.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often retrieve more candidates than they can pass to the downstream language model. A dedicated reranker helps select the most relevant candidates for the final context [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . This usually improves the quality of the retrieved context, but processing a large candidate set can add substantial latency. In practice, teams must balance relevance, response time and GPU resources. System-1-style decision models offer a possible alternative. Instead of generating a free-form answer, they return scores or selections over predefined options. Reranking can also be framed as choosing the best candidates from a set, so these models may be able to do the same job with less inference overhead. Yet specialized rerankers are built for relevance ranking, and a decision model must still process the query and every candidate text. A lower latency is therefore a hypothesis, not a given.

Finally, we test selected configurations on a new retrieval benchmark without retuning them. This design separates a model’s ability to rerank from its suitability as a production replacement.

passages.text: The broad screen cannot show whether replacement works, because its protocols differ. We therefore fixed one comparison before running the BRIGHT experiments, based on earlier exploratory runs. On a multi-hop task PPLX Decider v1.1 (revision 14c9d90) and Jina Reranker v3.5 were nearly tied (87.8% versus 88.8% conditional complete-support retention), on a synthetic enterprise task PPLX was ahead (92.1% versus 79.7%), and in an isolated serving test Jina was far faster (p95 86 versus 1,785 ms): a useful quality–latency trade-off to investigate, and both run on one A100. No completion-rate threshold governed the choice, and default PPLX completes only 44.1% of BRIGHT requests. We chose Jina over Qwen3-Reranker-4B as the incumbent because it led it in those runs, it reranks a Top-20 set in one request, and it later improved on the first-stage order on all 11 benchmarks. Carrying PPLX forward was outcome-informed: after default PPLX failed on long inputs and truncation rescued it, it was the only decision model taken through the order, two-stage, budget-sweep and transfer experiments, as a promising truncated decision-model configuration. Default Winnow-12B with a BM25 fallback scores higher on BRIGHT (0.2011 against 0.1928), and our records do not document why it was not carried forward. The case study tests a specific replacement hypothesis, not the model family or every reranker. The main comparison pits a 27B structured-decision model against a 0.6B dedicated reranker, not a parameter-matched test: the size difference is part of the deployment question. We match the candidate lists and, in controls, the candidate text.

System-1-style decision models can perform competitive RAG reranking, but they are not inherently better replacements for dedicated rerankers. Input handling decides whether a decision model is reliable, and a frozen evaluation on new data shows that one of two selected configurations meets all our replacement checks. Yet which model ranks better depends on the workload, and the gains can come with higher latency and far greater GPU memory use. Tuning the existing reranker offered the better trade-off. For production RAG, tune the incumbent first, then test any alternative on representative candidate sets, and replace it only when the complete reranking policy meets the system’s quality, reliability, latency and memory requirements.
